h1: Can or bottle for hot markets
title: Can or Bottle for Hot Markets | Craft Beer School
desc: Cans or bottles for beer sold in hot climates: light, oxygen, heat, weight, recycling and the cold chain, compared plainly.
teaser: Heat ages beer quickly. The pack you choose changes how well your beer survives the journey.
standfirst: There is no single right answer, but there are clear trade-offs. This guide compares cans and bottles for breweries selling where the weather is hot.
sections:
Warm storage speeds up every slow reaction in packaged beer. Hop aroma fades, a papery or wet cardboard note builds and sweetness can turn toward honey or sherry. These are oxidation and ageing effects. They run faster at 30 °C (86 °F) than at 5 °C (41 °F). A pallet left on a loading dock or in a hot van ages far faster than one kept cold. See beer off-flavours for how these notes taste.

So the question is less about which pack looks nicer and more about which one protects the beer from oxygen, light and warmth. It is also about which one the market can recycle.

Light striking hop compounds produces a skunky aroma in minutes. Clear and green glass offer little protection. Brown glass blocks much of the damaging light, though not all of it. A metal can blocks all of it.

In hot, bright climates, bottles sit in sunny shop windows and open-air markets. If you choose glass, choose brown and print clear instructions on the carton to keep the beer out of direct sun.

A crown cap liner is not a perfect barrier. Over months a small amount of oxygen passes through. Some liners include an oxygen scavenger to slow this. A can seam, when set correctly, is hermetic. The weak point on a can line is the fill itself. Dissolved oxygen picked up before seaming matters more than the can.

Whichever pack you choose, measure oxygen at fill. A small brewery can start with a handheld meter and a routine for purging cans or bottles with carbon dioxide before filling.

Cans are lighter, which lowers freight cost per litre and makes small deliveries by motorbike or van easier. They also cool faster in a chiller or a bucket of ice, which matters where customers want the beer cold within minutes. Bottles are heavier and break. A broken bottle in a hot truck is a mess and a safety risk.

Glass keeps cold well once it is cold. Neither pack survives a long spell in the sun, so the cold chain (chilled storage and transport from brewery to shelf) matters more than the pack.

Bottles need a bottler, crown caps, labels and a sanitised, rinsed supply of glass. Returnable bottles save money but need washing, inspection and a deposit scheme. Cans can be filled on small mobile lines that some regions offer as a service, which lets a brewery start without owning equipment. Printed cans have minimum order quantities, so check the volumes before you commit. Shrink sleeves allow small runs with full-colour design.

Both metal and glass are widely recyclable, but collection systems differ by country. Ask local recyclers what they accept and tell customers how to dispose of the pack. Design choices connect to marketing, since the pack is a medium you control.

Hop-forward beers suffer most from heat and oxygen, so they favour cans and a tight cold chain. Strong dark beers and some Belgian-style ales tolerate warmth better and age more gracefully. Beers that finish in the pack, such as bottle-conditioned ales, need glass or a can rated for the pressure and a producer who knows what they are doing.

Pasteurisation is another lever. A tunnel pasteuriser heats filled packs to kill microbes and extends shelf life, though it can change hop character. Whether it is worth it depends on how far and how warm the beer travels.

Sell mostly through chilled outlets within a short drive? Cans are lighter and protect from light. Sell through unchilled shops or ship long distances? Prioritise a low oxygen fill, pasteurise if you can and print a best-before date you trust. Run a test: store samples at the temperatures your beer will meet, taste them every two weeks and compare them with a refrigerated sample.

Choosing a pack involves design, cost and technical limits all at once. A course in beer branding and packaging covers materials, labels and design together, so that the decision is made once, with the whole picture in view.
faqs: Are cans better than bottles in hot countries?
Cans block light fully and are lighter. Bottles can work if brown glass and a good closure are used. Oxygen at fill and the cold chain matter more than the pack alone.
Does heat really age beer faster?
Yes. Chemical reactions that cause staling run faster at higher temperatures.
Not always. It extends shelf life where beer travels far or warm, but it adds equipment cost and can change flavour.
A properly lined can does not add a metallic taste. Poor fills and damaged liners can.
